newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Socialists musketeers out of wilderness.
newsitem.headline: French Socialists musketeers out of wilderness.

text.p: Socialist leader Lionel Jospin's "seven musketeers" fanned out across France on Wednesday, buoyed by an unexpected first-round performance and scenting a possible victory at hand in Sunday's parliamentary election runoff.
Jospin sent a handpicked team on an intense last-stretch campaign effort, holding rallies throughout the country and multiplying radio and television interviews.
For many, it was a swifter than expected return to the limelight from political wilderness.

Among them were former young stars whose rise under the late president Francois Mitterrand was halted by the Socialists' 1993 election disaster: former ministers such as Martine Aubry, Dominique Strauss-Kahn and Segolene Royal.

Now in their late 40s, the attractive "Mitterrand generation" pragmatists helped Jospin's presidential election bid two years ago but returned to relative obscurity after he lost to Gaullist President Jacques Chirac.
The snap election called by Chirac propelled them back to prominence, poised to regain their seats in the National Assembly and join the cabinet if the Socialists win.
Strauss-Kahn is the hot tip for finance minister and Aubry for a superministry of employment and social affairs.

The left scored a major upset in last Sunday's first round, outpolling the ruling centre-right by more than four points amid discontent over record unemployment and budget austerity imposed to qualify France for a single European currency.
Polling firms said the left was on course for a narrow majority if the pattern were repeated in Sunday's runoff.

Jospin also picked veteran Jack Lang, who was Mitterrand's culture minister for a decade, and former humanitarian affairs minister Bernard Kouchner, who won prominence by campaigning for the international community's right to intervene to protect civilians in civil wars and disasters.

The quixotic Kouchner's comeback is the most surprising. Earlier this year, the outspoken founder of the Medecins sans Frontieres medical relief organisation announced he was quitting politics after failing to find a constituency, and leaving for Sudan to return to his original job as an aid doctor.

Two new faces are among Jospin's musketeers: Catherine Trautmann, the dogged mayor of Strasbourg who has led resistance to the extreme-right National Front, and Nantes mayor Jean-Marc Ayrault, one of the few Socialists to keep his seat in 1993.
Former European affairs minister Elisabeth Guigou is not one of the "musketeers", but she has played a prominent campaign role, defending Jospin's conditions for a single European currency.

Jospin has also called on veteran Socialist heavyweights, giving campaign roles to former European commission president Jacques Delors, Aubry's father, and former prime ministers Michel Rocard, Pierre Mauroy and Laurent Fabius.
Fabius could be president of the National Assembly if the left wins, and Rocard has been tipped for foreign minister.
Delors has taken a back seat since deciding not to run in the 1995 presidential election, but he remains France's most popular politician and a valuable moral supporter for Jospin.

Rocard, who was prime minister in 1988-91, briefly led the Socialists after the 1993 defeat but was voted out amid factional recrimination after another rout in European Parliament elections the following year.
